claim: strata.json carries a metre label and a stratum code for 39,833 padas in 10,552 stanzas. The five uppercase codes and their five lowercase counterparts distribute as A 8,566 / S 9,340 / N 9,846 / C 6,670 / P 5,411 padas after case-folding.
notes: A count of the codes in the file. It is not a statement that the codes are chronological. Reproduces PUR-012's 39,833/10,552 exactly at a five-week interval and from a fresh clone.

claim: 3,608 of the 39,833 padas (9.06%) carry a lowercase stratum code, which Arnold uses for a period indicated by the metrical variations alone. The lowercase share is not spread evenly: book 9 has none at all, books 2 and 4 have 0.71% and 1.96%, and books 1 and 3 have 22.41% and 23.59%.
notes: Nearly a quarter of books 1 and 3 is assigned on Arnold's own weaker criterion, and book 9 on his stronger one throughout. A by-book comparison of strata is therefore also a comparison of assignment confidence, and no unit in this repository has controlled for that.

claim: Under Arnold's own instrument, mandala number carries essentially no signal about the share of late-stratum material. Spearman rho between book number and the Cretic-plus-Popular share of the book's padas is -0.0667, and 23 of the 45 book pairs are inverted against a monotone increase, where chance alone gives 22.5.
notes: This is the measured form of the instruction that mandala number is not a time axis. It is a statement about Arnold's instrument, not about the Rigveda: if the strata are chronological, book order is not; if book order is chronological, the strata are not. The two cannot both be read as chronologies of the same thing.

claim: By Arnold's late (Cretic plus Popular) pada share the ten books rank: book 8 4.40%, book 9 5.82%, book 4 5.83%, book 2 15.41%, book 3 24.23%, book 6 30.32%, book 5 31.05%, book 7 31.25%, book 1 33.95%, book 10 74.79%. Corpus 30.33%.
notes: Books 8 and 9, which constitution 4.A calls internally complicated, carry the LOWEST late share in the corpus. Books 5, 6 and 7 - family books - carry a late share within three points of book 1. Only book 10 separates sharply. Whatever the family-book grouping is tracking, Arnold's metrical lateness is not it.

claim: Arnold's strata are not all present in all books. No pada of books 3, 4 or 7 is coded Archaic; no pada of book 6 is coded Strophic; no pada of books 4 or 8 is coded Cretic. Books 1, 2, 5, 9 and 10 carry all five.
notes: Under a strictly chronological reading this says books 3, 4 and 7 contain not one archaic pada, and books 4 and 8 not one Cretic pada. That is a strong empirical claim about the corpus. Under a metrical-genre reading it is unremarkable. The strata layer does not distinguish the two readings and neither can this repository.

claim: The metre label alone does not determine the stratum code: across all 66 metre labels the modal stratum accounts for 42.36% of padas, and for the largest label M (25,655 padas) only 26.96%. But at the edges the two are near-identical: the labels P, PE1, PE2 and PE3b (4,200 padas together) are 99.9-100% Popular.
notes: The first half of this measurement defends Arnold: the stratum is not a relabelling of the surface metre, so he was using finer metrical facts. The second half is the confound: the Popular stratum is substantially co-extensive with a set of metre labels, so a claim that material is late because it is Popular is close to a claim that it is late because of its metre. Both halves are the result.

claim: No stanza mixes uppercase and lowercase stratum codes across its padas, which reproduces PUR-012 exactly (9,607 all-uppercase, 945 all-lowercase, 10,552 total). Two stanzas mix stratum LETTERS: RV 1.30.22 has S S C and RV 9.71.9 has S S S N.
notes: Not a correction of PUR-012, which was about case and is right. It is a separate fact PUR-012 did not state, and it matters for any unit that aggregates pada-level strata to the stanza: the aggregation is lossless for 10,550 stanzas and lossy for two. The pur- corpus reported zero non-uniform passages among its 103, which is consistent with this.

claim: The five stanza-properties columns flag, out of 10,552 stanzas: Grassmann 1,094 (10.37%), Arnold-Sketch 1,308 (12.40%), Wuest 709 (6.72%), Oldenberg 699 (6.62%), Witzel 689 (6.53%). 2,372 stanzas (22.48%) are flagged by at least one.
notes: Binary presence only. What the letter codes w W G z Z o O C1 C2 distinguish is undocumented in the bundle (manifest, 'What is not documented'), so this unit reads the columns as flags and throws the letters away.

claim: Oldenberg and Wuest flag almost the same stanzas: 641 shared of 699 and 709, Jaccard 0.8357, 91.7% of Oldenberg inside Wuest and 90.4% the reverse. No other pair exceeds Jaccard 0.49.
notes: DEP-030. The four non-Arnold columns are not four instruments. Witzel sits at Jaccard 0.486 with Oldenberg and 0.476 with Wuest; Grassmann is the most distinct of the five, at 0.19-0.25 against every other column.

claim: Every one of the five columns is enriched in Arnold's late strata. Share of a column's flagged stanzas falling in Cretic or Popular, against a corpus rate of 29.0%: Arnold-Sketch 94.12%, Wuest 76.73%, Oldenberg 76.11%, Witzel 61.39%, Grassmann 52.97%. Yates-corrected chi-square on 1 df: 3031.6, 838.4, 804.4, 374.0, 339.1.
notes: Enrichment against a corpus baseline, not against a matched control. The single number that matters is Grassmann's, because Grassmann is the one column that is neither Arnold nor entangled with Oldenberg.

claim: The enrichment survives removing book 10. Within books 1-9 only, where the base late rate is 19.71%, the enrichment ratios are Arnold-Sketch 4.59, Wuest 3.56, Oldenberg 3.54, Witzel 2.77, Grassmann 2.34. Within book 10 alone, where the base rate is 75.6%, every ratio collapses to between 0.89 and 1.29.
notes: The control DEP-004 demands, run. The agreement between Arnold's metre and four earlier scholars' judgements is NOT an artifact of book 10 being both late and heavily flagged. Inside book 10 the flags carry almost no information about the stratum, which is the same fact seen from the other side.

claim: Grassmann 1876-7 - the one flagging instrument that is neither Arnold nor near-identical to another column - marks 46.12% of its books 1-9 stanzas inside Arnold's late strata against a 19.71% base, a ratio of 2.34.
notes: This is the strongest single result of the unit in Arnold's favour and it is one instrument, from 1876-7, whose criterion is undocumented in the bundle. It is not a replication of Arnold and it is not nothing.

claim: 94.12% of the 1,293 stanzas flagged in the Arnold-Sketch column fall in Arnold's late strata, the highest of the five columns and 17 points above the next.
notes: DEP-035. The measured form of DEP-022. Arnold 1897 on grammar and Arnold 1905 on metre agree about which stanzas are late far more closely than any two different scholars do.

claim: The flags are not evenly distributed by book. In book 10 the Arnold-Sketch column flags 44.58% of stanzas and at least one column flags 57.47%; in book 9 at least one column flags 6.32%.
notes: Book 10 is where five scholars working from grammar, style, translation, textual criticism and history converge, independently of Arnold's metre. It is the one place in the corpus where the instruments agree strongly.

claim: 7,602 of 10,552 stanzas (72.04%) differ between the transmitted Samhitapatha (Aufrecht) and the metrically restored text (van Nooten and Holland 1994) once whitespace and pada division are removed. In 5,246 of those (69.01%) the restored text is LONGER than the transmitted one.
notes: Constitution 4.A's 'later sandhi or contraction that may obscure an older metrical form', measured. Inspected instances: RV 1.1.2 i-dyo > i-diyo, 1.1.6 tvam > tuvam, 1.1.9 sva- > sua- and 'gne > agne with the elision undone, 1.2.1 darsate me > darsata ime. The restoration is overwhelmingly a matter of putting syllables back.

claim: The gap between the transmitted and the restored text is roughly flat across Arnold's strata and is largest in the Archaic: Archaic 77.20% of stanzas differ, Cretic 74.81%, Strophic 70.04%, Popular 69.57%, Normal 69.13%.
notes: The recitational overlay is corpus-wide, not a property of late material. The stratum Arnold calls oldest needs the MOST restoration. That is what a uniform later phonology applied across material of different ages would look like, and it is also what a metrical instrument reading through that overlay has to cope with.

claim: By book, the share of stanzas differing between transmitted and restored text runs from 63.09% (book 9) to 78.24% (book 7); the family books 2-7 range 68.56-78.24% and books 8-10 range 63.09-73.43%.
notes: No book is exempt. The narrow range is the point: the Samhitapatha applies one phonology to the whole corpus.

claim: The recited Samhitapatha is recoverable letter-for-letter from the padapatha in 22 of 10,552 stanzas (0.21%) once accents are stripped from both, and in 27 (0.26%) once the padapatha's inserted iti-material is also removed. Median character-level similarity between the two strings is 0.913 and the mean is 0.910.
notes: The padapatha is an ANALYSIS, not a segmentation: it splits compounds, inserts iti after certain words and restores pre-sandhi shapes, so the 99.8% is not 99.8% sandhi. The similarity figure is the usable number: about 9% of the segmental material of the recited text is not letter-for-letter present in the word-analysis of the same stanza.

claim: The Rigveda holds two complete transmitted forms of the same text that disagree with each other at almost every stanza, and a third, modern, reconstructed form that disagrees with both.
locator: 04-AUDITS/domain-a-tables/A6a-samhita-vs-restored-by-book.csv and A7-padapatha-vs-samhita.csv taken together; the third comparison, padapatha against restored text, differs at 99.84% of stanzas
notes: Recorded because it is the fact that both traps in constitution 4.A deny. A perfect audio recording would not need a padapatha and would not admit a metrical restoration; a rewritten text would not preserve, inside its own tradition, a second analysis that contradicts the first at nine tenths of its stanzas.
